newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First pitches to nationalist vote.
newsitem.headline: NZ First pitches to nationalist vote.

text.p: For the first time in a week, it did not rain on opposition New Zealand First leader Winston Peters' party in Auckland on Monday.
Eschewing the stage-managed halls of the other main parties' openings, economic nationalist New Zealand First launched its election campaign in downtown Auckland's Queen Elizabeth Square.
Forecast light rain stayed away, but the event was overshadowed by the recent resignation of two candidates and public differences between Peters and his deputy Tau Henare.
Henare last week ruled out working in coalition with the governing National Party, contradicting the party line which was to leave all coalitions open until after the October 12 election.

But at the campaign launch Peters seemed to side with the sentiment, if not the letter, of Henare's position in a speech dominated by attacks on the National government and big business, which he said backed National.
With his black and white campaign bus, "Kiwi Spirit" as the centrepiece, he told a lunchtime crowd of about 1,000 the campaign would be "about who owns New Zealand".

"We are not a party that sells this country off to foreigners and rich corporates," he said, cataloguing the "roll of shame" of $16 billion in asset sales by the National government and its Labour predecessor.
He said a National government would continue the sales and make New Zealanders "virtual peasants in our own land".
He promised a society "that does not kowtow to rich tax- concealing corporates or to foreigners who want to own our country".
"New Zealand First is not for the rich corporates who hide their tax millions in the Cook Islands and rob the New Zealand people blind and expect knighthoods at home," Peters said.
Nor was it for "the reef-fish' and the selfish financial markets...and the power-hungry Business Roundtable and their political mates".
He touched only lightly on the party's stand on health, education and unemployment and said New Zealand First had the policies to fix high interest rates and a sagging economy.

New Zealand First is the last of the four major parties to officially launch, but its campaign has run into early problems. Last week two Wellington candidates quit over their low rankings on the party's list and amid allegations that Peters' longtime friend and special adviser Michael Laws had too much influence and was moving policy closer to that of the ruling National Party.
Then Henare publicly ruled out working with the governing National Party after the election, saying he would take a back seat if the party opted for a deal with National.
But Henare told Reuters on Monday he would not give up the deputy's position without a fight.
"I'm a team player. I'll do what the caucus wants," he said. "But I haven't fought for three years to give that (the deputy leadership) up."
He said if New Zealand First went into coalition with National he would not serve in Cabinet.
On current polling the government and its likely partners have 45 percent support and the three main opposition parties more than 50 percent combined.
Of the three, only New Zealand First has not ruled out a deal with National after the election.
